newsitem.title: UK: UK govt has headstart in funding 1997-98 deficit.
newsitem.headline: UK govt has headstart in funding 1997-98 deficit.

text.p: By Cheryl Juckes,
The British government has a headstart in its 1997-98 funding programme after borrowing more than necessary to cover the previous fiscal year's budget deficit, data published on Wednesday suggest.
"They're going to be carrying forward an overfund of something around three or four billion stg," said Societe Generale economist Tom Rayner.
"The pressure's really been removed."

Analysts say the Bank of England made gross government bond (gilt) sales of around 39.0 billion stg in fiscal 1996-97, to fund the central government borrowing requirement (CGBR), cover redemptions of maturing gilts and an underfund of 2.2 billion carried forward from fiscal 1995-96.
But the level of gilt sales was based on an estimate of a CGBR of 27.9 billion stg for fiscal 1996-97 when the actual outturn was 25.1 billion pounds.

Rayner estimates this means the Bank of England will only have to sell around 33.0 billion stg of gilts to fund the 1997-98 deficit, instead of the 36.5 billion implied by the official CGBR forecast of 20.0 billion.
"We could see them going for the minumum at gilt auctions rather than the maximum. We may even have one auction pulled," Rayner said.
The Bank of England has said there will be 11 auctions in the current fiscal year and it can also raise funds through less formal tap sales.
The auction size can range from 2.0 to 3.0 billion stg for single stock auctions and 3.0 to 4.5 billion for the four dual auctions planned.
HSBC bond economist Don Smith estimates the overfund for fiscal 1996-97 is actually 4.7 billion stg, once sales of national savings products and changes in official reserves are taken into account.

"They've actually done extremely well. But I think they would prefer to stick to the schedule and get the market used to regular auctions so I think they'll simply go for smaller amounts at each," he said.

Smith said that Britain had sold around 900 million U.S. dollars of its official reserves of foreign currency in the 1996-97 fiscal year, putting around 600 million stg extra in its coffers and further offsetting the need to borrow.
He also said that the government would probably have raised 5.0 billion stg in fiscal 1996-97 from sales of National Savings products rather than the 4.5 billion it estimated at the budget.
"I don't think the market has fully taken on board the extent to which the Bank has overfunded," Smith said.
He said the market was concerned about funding because in value terms 20 percent of the market was due to mature over the next three years.
Gilt redemptions will be 20 billion stg for fiscal 1997-98, 18 billion for 1998-99 and 15 billion in 2000, compared with total gilt market capitalisation of 260 billion, Smith said.
The overfund should go some way to assuaging worries about how government borrowing is to financed and will underpin sentiment.
But in a climate of rising U.S. interest rates, gilt yields are still likely to pick up.
"We will make some progress in spread terms but in absolute terms we're likely to see rising yields," Rayner said.
